newsitem.title: GERMANY: German regional metalworkers adjourn pay talks.
newsitem.headline: German regional metalworkers adjourn pay talks.

text.p: German metal and engineering workers and employers in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg on Tuesday adjourned pay talks after failing to agree on how to finance the maintenance of full sick pay.
A new law introduced in October allowed employers to reduce sick pay from its current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

But following mass protests and the threat of strikes in the already hard-hit industry, most of Germany's engineering firms have now backed away from enshrining the law in worker contracts and instead agreed to cut labour costs in other ways.

But in Nordwuerttemberg, employers are still holding out for tougher terms than those secured in other sectoral pay deals across the country, most notably in a break-through deal in the state of Lower Saxony. All the deals have involved the maintenance of 100 percent sick pay.
After Tuesday's meeting was adjourned until Wednesday, regional employers' negotiator Klaus Fritsche said the IG Metall union had not offered enough in the way of compensation.
But IG Metall negotiator Gerhard Zambelli said he had been surprised the employers had chosen an adjournment rather than pressing on at once. "We came a very long way," he said.

In the two weeks since the Lower Saxony deal, contracts securing full sick pay have been signed for two-thirds of the 3.2 million workers in the west German metal and engineering sectors. Nordwuerttemberg is home to another 600,000 workers.
Zambelli said the main bone of contention now was how much of employees' overtime or weekend bonuses should continue to be taken into account in calculating sick pay.

The Lower Saxony agreement, which has been adopted by regions including the steel-producing state of North Rhine-Westphalia and the large Bavarian engineering region, includes a 1.5 pay rise next year and 2.5 percent in 1998.

Taking into account small reductions in worker bonuses that employers have been able to secure, the accords are calculated to increase labour costs in the industry by less than one percent next year, and by slightly more in 1998.

While significantly lower than the wage deal agreed for 1996, it means that employers will once again have failed to bring in the deep reduction in labour costs they have for years been crying out for.
